Keeper of the Gulls’ Watch

On a jagged promontory where wind-whipped waves crashed like drums against black stone, stood Gull’s Watch Lighthouse. Every night, Thomas Marlowe climbed its spiral staircase, lantern in hand, to trim the wick and polish the great Fresnel lens. He had tended that beacon for more than twenty years, ever since inheriting the post from his father.

The cape was lonely. During daylight hours, Thomas performed small repairs—recaulking seams, oiling hinges, dusting the narrow windowsills where barnacle-chirped gulls nested. He’d learned to read the sea’s moods in the gulls’ cries: a sudden, sharp squawk meant an offshore storm gathering; a chorus of soft coos meant calm waters near.

One autumn evening, a fierce gale rose without warning. Thomas lit the lamp as dusk bled into slate-gray clouds. He fought against the howling wind to secure the door, then yanked hard at the lantern’s lever, channeling a ribbon of golden light through the storm. For six hours, he wedged himself against the railing, checking every bolt, willing the storm to spare passing ships.

Around midnight, through his fogged window, he spotted a tiny silhouette battered by waves—a fishing sloop gone astray. Heart pounding, Thomas signaled with an emergency lantern code: three long flashes, one pause, two flashes. He raced below, threw on oilskins, and rowed into the dark spray, following his own beam like a guardian’s guiding star. The captain of the sloop, disoriented and exhausted, steered alongside. Thomas helped haul them aboard his sturdy dinghy and brought them back to the safety of the lighthouse’s broad base.

By dawn, the storm had spent itself, and exhausted survivors cozied up beside Thomas’s hearth. He brewed tea and offered dry blankets as gulls wheeled overhead, their cries softer now under a timid sunrise. The crew set out again once the sea calmed, waving thanks as their little vessel rejoined the horizon.

Years later, the rescued captain would tell his grandchildren about the quiet man in the lighthouse who fought the storm’s fury with nothing more than unwavering courage and a steadfast light. And though Thomas Marlowe’s name faded into time, the beacon he kept still shines on stormy nights, a promise that even in darkness, someone watches, someone cares.
